title: Katyal's Boast of AI Role in Tariff Win Draws Swift Blowback
author: Jordan Fischer

kp.k: Katyal reports AI-assisted Supreme Court argument preparation
kp.d: The article reports that Milbank partner Neal Katyal used Harvey alongside mindfulness, improv and meditation coaches to prepare his November argument against President Donald Trump’s tariffs. Katyal described a bespoke system trained on 25 years of Supreme Court papers that could anticipate questions and opinions. The court ruled 6-3 for the challenging businesses; the account reports Katyal’s claims rather than establishing that AI caused the victory.
qs: Rather it was about the four coaches he’d brought onboard to help him prepare to better connect with the justices: a mindfulness coach who had worked with tennis great Andre Agassi, an improv coach, a meditation coach, and Harvey, the AI model he said helped him anticipate the justices’ thinking.
a “bespoke AI system” trained on 25 years of Supreme Court papers that was able to predict not just the justices’ questions, but their eventual opinions.

kp.k: Question prediction and strategic influence remain advocate-reported claims
kp.d: In his TED Talk, Katyal compared Harvey’s predicted questions with oral argument excerpts and said some were almost verbatim. He also credited Harvey with identifying an argument that could bring Chief Justice John Roberts to his side. These are Katyal’s demonstrations and interpretation of the tool’s contribution, not an independently measured prediction-performance result.
qs: In the TED Talk, Katyal displayed Harvey’s predicted questions alongside excerpts from the actual oral argument transcript, saying some were “almost verbatim.”
He also credited the tool with identifying an “escape route” to bring Chief Justice John Roberts to his side in the case.
“Harvey glimpsed that narrow door, I held the door open, the Chief Justice walked through it,” Katyal said.

kp.k: Digital moot courts could become increasingly common
kp.d: University of Virginia Supreme Court Litigation Clinic director Xiao Wang predicted increasing use of AI for digital moot courts and reported having used it himself. Separately, Harvey said its technology had been used to prepare for at least one other Supreme Court case that term. The article thus combines a practitioner’s experience and forecast with a vendor-reported adoption claim, rather than providing profession-wide adoption measurements.
qs: But Wang predicted Supreme Court advocates will increasingly use the technology for digital moot courts, as he himself has, if many aren’t already doing so.
Harvey says its client list includes Walmart Inc., Comcast Corp., and O’Melveny & Myers, and that it’s been used to prep for at least one other Supreme Court case this term.

kp.k: Critics challenge AI-centered accounts of collective litigation success
kp.d: The article places Katyal’s personal account against the involvement of multiple elite firms and dozens of amicus briefs. Daniel Epps questioned the suggestion that AI and coaching were decisive; Wang stressed that oral advocates are only one part of securing a win. The article also notes that Katyal credited his legal team, Colleen Roh Sinzdak and the Liberty Justice Center in a promotional social media post.
qs: It’s unusual to see an advocate like Katyal take such personal credit for a win at the Supreme Court, and his remarks prompted pushback from court watchers, particularly considering the case in question involved multiple elite law firms and dozens of amicus briefs.

“The notion that it’s Katyal’s preparation with his mindfulness coach and AI that was the key difference maker, I just think people think that was a little preposterous,” said Daniel Epps, a professor at the Washington University School of Law in St. Louis.
“I thought it was a little strange for the quarterback here to say there is in fact an ‘I’ in team,” Wang said.

kp.k: Claims of AI-enabled persuasion may carry reputational risks
kp.d: Epps argued that Katyal’s comments sounded arrogant and could damage his credibility with the justices by implying he could manipulate them and change their votes. This is a critic’s assessment of professional reputational risk, not a reported reaction from the justices or an established consequence.
qs: Epps, who clerked for Justice Anthony Kennedy, echoed other critics who said the comments came across as “arrogant” and could undermine Katyal’s standing with the justices.
“I think he’s really damaged his credibility with them,” Epps said, adding Katyal sounded as though he was saying he was able to manipulate the justices and change their votes.

kp.k: Prediction tools may complement high-stakes advocacy skills
kp.d: University of Virginia professor Mitu Gulati saw potential value in AI identifying patterns in judicial questioning and reasoning, treating such predictability as reassuring evidence of consistency rather than simply predetermined outcomes. He qualified this favorable interpretation by allowing that Katyal may have overstated AI’s role and expressing doubt that oral argument changed a vote, while emphasizing the value of an advocate capable of doing so.
qs: Still, Katyal’s presentation underscored the potential value of AI-driven prediction tools, according to Mitu Gulati, a University of Virginia law professor who studies the Supreme Court.
Advocates prize consistency from the justices, Gulati said, and the fact that an AI model could identify patterns in their questioning and reasoning was reassuring.
“Everybody reads everything and it’s hard to imagine oral argument changed anybody’s vote,” Gulati said. “That said, if you can change a vote, that’s why you pay the guy.”

kp.k: Harvey denies financial or promotional ties to Katyal
kp.d: A Harvey spokeswoman said Katyal had no arrangement to promote the company’s services and held no investment or equity stake. This vendor statement provides context for his public endorsement; the article reports that Katyal did not respond to requests for comment.
qs: A spokeswoman for Harvey said in an email it has no arrangement with Katyal to promote its services and he doesn’t hold any investment or equity stake in the company.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source describes AI-assisted Supreme Court preparation, predicts wider use of digital moot courts, and reports competing assessments of AI's contribution to litigation outcomes.
pts.d: Jordan Fischer reports that rapid adoption of AI tools has upended the legal industry and that fabricated case citations create difficulties for courts. Neal Katyal claims that a bespoke Harvey AI system helped anticipate the justices' questions and eventual opinions, with some predicted questions matching oral argument almost verbatim. He also credits it with identifying an argumentative route to secure Chief Justice Roberts's support. Xiao Wang predicts increasing use of AI for digital moot courts by Supreme Court advocates. Mitu Gulati interprets the presentation as illustrating the potential value of AI prediction tools in identifying consistency in judicial questioning and reasoning. Daniel Epps disputes the portrayal of Katyal's AI-assisted preparation as the decisive factor and warns that the presentation could damage Katyal's credibility with the justices. These are attributed assessments, not a demonstrated causal finding that AI changed the outcome.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists principally of Katyal's case account and selected transcript comparisons, Wang's personal experience, Harvey's reported usage, and expert commentary.
pts.d: Katyal's supporting demonstration juxtaposed Harvey's predicted questions with actual oral argument excerpts. The article reports training on 25 years of Supreme Court papers and the coalition's 6–3 victory, but supplies no systematic accuracy benchmark, full prediction set, or comparison establishing that AI caused the result. Wang grounds his adoption prediction partly in his own use of digital moot courts. Harvey reports use in at least one additional Supreme Court case that term and names corporate and law-firm clients; these are company statements rather than independently measured adoption rates. Gulati offers an interpretation based on his study of the Court. Epps and Wang emphasize the limitations of attributing a team litigation outcome to one advocate's preparation, while Gulati questions how often oral argument changes votes. Fischer's broad industry-disruption statement is not accompanied by quantified adoption evidence in the captured text.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern reported current use in the 2026 article and an undated prediction of expanding adoption, with qualifications about bespoke preparation and uncertain influence on votes.
pts.d: Katyal describes preparation for the tariff case he argued in November, before the reported decision and 2026 TED Talk. Harvey's additional use claim concerns the same Supreme Court term. Wang predicts increasing adoption without a numerical target or deadline and allows that many advocates may already use the technology. Katyal's specific predictive claims concern a bespoke system trained on Supreme Court materials, not AI tools generally. Gulati accepts potential predictive value even if Katyal overstated the system's role, while qualifying the possibility that oral advocacy changes votes. The article describes present assistance to human advocates, not autonomous representation or replacement of lawyers.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are Supreme Court advocates and their litigation teams, high-stakes clients, and courts.
pts.d: For Supreme Court advocates, the claimed benefit is additional preparation through simulated questioning, anticipation of judicial reasoning, and identification of persuasive arguments. The tariff litigation illustrates potential relevance to business clients in high-stakes disputes, but the article does not establish a separate client benefit caused by AI. Litigation teams remain important: Wang stresses that the oral advocate is only one contributor. Courts face difficulties from fabricated citations, while justices are the subjects of prediction and the audience whose trust Epps says Katyal risks damaging through his public claims. Harvey is identified as the legal-AI vendor supplying the tool, and its named customers include corporations and a law firm. The captured text makes no concrete prediction about legal employment, staffing structures, fees, or access to justice.
